text.p: Australian-based softdrink bottler Coca-Cola Amatil Ltd saw A$1 billion (US$770 million) wiped off its market capitalisation last week as investors reacted to its 1996 results and expansion into Eastern Europe.

The market capitalisation of the former darling of the Australian stock market and the world's second largest Coke bottler has now dropped more than A$3 billion, about a third of its former value, since it alerted the market to a flat full year result last November.
The share price has plummeted from a closing high of A$18 in mid-October to A$11.80 at Friday's close, after dipping as low as $A11.15 during the week.
"The market has got itself to blame for rating the stock so highly, given that it was very much in a start-up phase in Europe," said Peter Morgan, head of equities at Perpetual Funds Management.
The sharp fall has polarised analysts, with one influential report putting fair value at A$10.20 at best, while others have buy or accumulate recommendations above A$13 a share.

Shares in C-C Amatil, about 36 percent owned by giant The Coca-Cola Co, took off in mid-1995 and rose steadily as institutions chased one of the few local blue-chip stocks seen as offering long-term growth.
The company expanded rapidly in Asia and Eastern Europe, picking up franchises in countries such as Ukraine and Croatia and spending A$800 million last year on plant and equipment.

The share price was given a filip last August when C-C Amatil placed about 9.3 percent of its shares with Robert Kuok's Hong Kong-based Kerry Group, seen as boosting its chances of entering the vast Chinese market.
Senior executives spoke of 1996 percentage profit growth in the "mid-teens".

The first chinks in its armour appeared after an analysts and investors tour to Eastern Europe last October. Stockbroker First Pacific issued a report which assigned a fair value to C-C Amatil of just A$12.50, about A$5 below its then quoted price. Its concerns centred on the cost of developing franchises, ineffective marketing strategies and overestimation of sales growth.

But the shares held steady until mid-November when C-C Amatil revealed that the drive to enter new territories and boost market share had cut margins and eaten into profits. A statement saying calendar 1996 profits would show little change on 1995 prompted a 25 percent slump in the share price.
Analysts said there was a perception C-C Amatil had been funding expansion of the U.S. parent by putting in all the capital expenditure and wearing all the losses from the market share battle.

The share price hovered around the A$13 mark, but slumped again this week after the company released its 1996 results. While the net profit showed a slight rise to A$142 million, meeting the revised forecast, analysts quickly suggested the figure had been boosted by a lower tax rate and the inclusion of a one-off payment as interest income.

First Pacific downgraded fair value to just A$9.20, with another A$1 for future franchise acquisitions. "We still believe there is further correction to go," said First Pacific food analyst Mike Jenneke.

Analysts noted that despite its share slide in recent months, the stock remains on a price earnings ratio of about 38, more than double the average for Australian industrial companies of about 16.5, and is likely to face further volatility.
"I don't think right now it's going to stabilise," said Macquarie Equities food analyst Raewyn Ellis-Doff. "There's too much worry and poor sentiment out there."
